etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Of the noun: from Middle English effect, from Old French effect (modern French effet), from Latin effectus (“an effect, tendency, purpose”), from efficiō (“accomplish, complete, effect”); see effect as a verb. Displaced Old English fremming, fremednes from fremman.

Of the verb: from Middle English effecten, partly from Medieval Latin effectuō, from Latin effectus, perfect passive participle of efficiō (“accomplish, complete, do, effect”), from ex (“out”) + faciō (“do, make”) (see fact and compare affect, infect) and partly from the noun effect.

definitions.definition: The result or outcome of a cause.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter I, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The stories did not seem to me to touch life. They were plainly intended to have a bracing moral effect, and perhaps had this result for the people at whom they were aimed.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 1, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: The half-dozen pieces  […]  were painted white and carved with festoons of flowers, birds and cupids.  […]   The bed was the most extravagant piece.  Its graceful cane halftester rose high towards the cornice and was so festooned in carved white wood that the effect was positively insecure, as if the great couch were trimmed with icing sugar.

quote.citation: 2013 June 8, “Obama goes troll-hunting”, in The Economist‎[2], volume 407, number 8839, page 55:
quote.text: The solitary, lumbering trolls of Scandinavian mythology would sometimes be turned to stone by exposure to sunlight. Barack Obama is hoping that several measures announced on June 4th will have a similarly paralysing effect on their modern incarnation, the patent troll.

definitions.definition: Impression left on the mind; sensation produced.

quote.citation: 1832 October, unknown author, “The Tears of Parents”, in The Christian Observer, volume 32:
1832, Washington Irving, Tales of the Alhambra:
quote.text: The effect was heightened by the wild and lonely nature of the place.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The state of being binding and enforceable, as in a rule, policy, or law.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene v]:
quote.text: That no compunctious visitings of nature / Shake my fell purpose, nor keep peace between / The effect and it.

definitions.definition: (cinematography, computer graphics, demoscene) An illusion produced by technical means (as in "special effect")

quote.citation: 2018, Jimmy Maher, The Future Was Here: The Commodore Amiga, page 186:
quote.text: The colored bands of color that strobe through much of the text and other visual elements are perhaps the most prototypical of all Amiga demoscene effects and, again, are a direct result of the hardware on which Megademo was created to run.

definitions.definition: (sound engineering) An alteration, or device for producing an alteration, in sound after it has been produced by an instrument.
(sciences) A scientific phenomenon, usually named after its discoverer.
(sciences, statistics) An influence or causal association between two variables.
(usually in the plural) Belongings, usually as personal effects.

quote.citation: 1690, “A Relation of the Late Great Revolution in Siam, and the Driving Out of the French”, in A Full and True Relation of the Great and Wonderful Revolution That Hapned Lately in the Kingdom of Siam in the East-Indies, London: Randal Taylor, page 7:
quote.text: His Goods, Family, and all his Effects were also ſeiz'd every where, and his Family carried into Priſon.

definitions.definition: Consequence intended; purpose; meaning; general intent; with to.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Chronicles 34:22:
quote.text: They spake to her to that effect.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Reality; actual meaning; fact, as distinguished from mere appearance.

quote.text: no other in effect than what it seems

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: All the large effects / That troop with majesty.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make or bring about; to implement.

quote.citation: 1828, Thomas Keightley, The Fairy Mythology, volume I, London: William Harrison Ainsworth, page 57:
quote.text: The offence thus given naturally effected an entire conversion in the queen's sentiments, and when Arthur returned from hunting, like Potiphar's wife, she charges Launfal with attempting her honour.

quote.citation: 1927, Havelock Ellis, Studies in the Psychology of Sex, Volume 2 (of 6)‎[3]:
quote.text: The punishment for sodomy, when completely effected, was death, and it was frequently inflicted.

quote.citation: 1944 July and August, Charles E. Lee, “The "City of Truro"”, in Railway Magazine, page 202:
quote.text: The transfer by tender of some 1,300 mail bags was effected smartly, and the "Ocean Mails Special" train was ready at 9.19 a.m.
